summary.text: In 79 AD, Mount Vesuvius, a stratovolcano in Campania, Italy, erupted in one of the deadliest eruptions in history.
It hurled super-heated tephra and gases 33 km high, and pyroclastic surges and falling ash buried Roman towns, most famously Pompeii and Herculaneum.
Excavations have revealed much of these towns and their people's lives, and Pliny the Younger left a detailed eyewitness account in two letters.

facts.label: Energy released
facts.value: 100,000 times the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings

facts.label: Remains found
facts.value: Over 1,500 people at Pompeii and Herculaneum

facts.label: Eyewitness
facts.value: Pliny the Younger, watching from Misenum

items.prompt: At Pompeii, archaeologists made plaster casts showing the exact poses of victims. How was that possible?

options.label: The bodies turned to stone over time
Thick ash sealed the bodies, leaving hollows
Lava froze around them like a mould
Rain turned the dust into a hard mud

items.explain: A thick ash layer sealed many bodies in cavities that kept their shapes, which later allowed plaster casts.

items.prompt: Small earthquakes shook the area for four days before the eruption, yet people did not treat them as a warning. Why?

options.label: They struck only at night while people slept
The emperor ordered everyone to ignore them
They were thought to bring good harvests
Tremors were common there, so they seemed normal

items.explain: Locals were used to minor tremors, which Pliny said were not alarming because they were frequent in Campania.

items.prompt: Many people who stayed in the towns into the next morning died. What killed them?

options.label: A slow river of lava
A tsunami from the bay
A fast, very hot pyroclastic flow
Hunger after roads were blocked

items.explain: In the early morning a rapid, dense and very hot pyroclastic flow knocked down walls and incinerated or suffocated the remaining population.

items.prompt: Early in the eruption, ash and pumice rained heavily on Pompeii but not on nearby Herculaneum. Why?

options.label: Herculaneum was upwind of the column
Herculaneum had stronger stone roofs
Hills blocked the ash from Herculaneum
Herculaneum was on the far side of the bay

items.explain: The early column of ash and pumice drifted southeast onto Pompeii, while Herculaneum lay upwind.

items.prompt: This eruption gave its name to the Vesuvian type of eruption. What marks that type?

options.label: Gentle fountains of runny lava
Hot gas and ash columns reaching the stratosphere
Steam bursts from melting glaciers
Lava lakes that slowly fill a crater

items.explain: Vesuvian eruptions are characterised by columns of hot gases and ash that reach the stratosphere.

items.prompt: What is thought to have supplied much of the explosive energy behind the 79 AD blast?

options.label: Seawater meeting hot magma and turning to steam
Strong winds blowing down into the crater
A large meteor striking the summit
Rainwater soaking into fresh ash on the slopes

items.explain: The eruption is considered mainly phreatomagmatic: seawater seeped into deep faults, met hot magma, and the escaping steam drove the blast.
